pages.title: OBSERVING THE MRT & ITS SURROUNDINGS.
pages.intro: Our first fieldwork: observing station access, pedestrian movement, crossings and routes around Dhoby Ghaut.

sections.name: Original Photos Left / Fieldwork Notes Right

children.name: Five photos stacked / tap to switch

children.text:
After our site visit, I noticed that the junction was quite complicated. There were a lot of cars and people, and it was noisy. I think this could make independent travel difficult for some autistic people, especially those who are sensitive to noise and crowds.

I also couldn’t see clear signs showing the way to Temasek Shophouse. Even if the route is physically accessible, finding the right direction is not always easy.
✳  CLEAR ROUTES MATTER AS MUCH AS ACCESSIBLE ONES.

pages.title: LISTEN TO THE PERSON, NOT THE LABEL.
pages.intro: Interviews and hands-on experiences gave us a better picture of how differently people move through and understand the same environment.

sections.name: Photos Left / Week 02 Interview Notes Right

children.name: Week 02 / Tap for Next Photo (Independent Component)

children.text: Through talking with people with visual impairment, I learned that some rely on sound, touch or familiar cues to understand their surroundings.
The wheelchair users we spoke with said they did not always like asking others for help. When they really needed it, they might prefer someone they knew or a staff member.

We also briefly experienced navigating without sight and using a wheelchair. Simple tasks felt less straightforward when we needed different routes, cues or support. This short exercise could not replace anyone’s lived experience, but it helped us see the environment differently.
Ask first. Listen carefully. Let people choose.

pages.title: BEYOND WHAT I SEE.
pages.intro: Interviews and an MRT encounter made me rethink what careful observation means.

sections.name: Week 03 / Photos Left · Interview Notes Right

children.name: Week 03 / Tap for Next Photo (Independent Component)

children.text: Through our conversations with autistic people, I learned that everyone has their own thoughts, feelings and ways of experiencing the world. I used to pay attention to behaviours I didn’t understand. Listening to their stories helped me focus more on the people behind those behaviours.

When we asked a wheelchair user about travelling by MRT, she told us that getting on and off the train was one of her biggest difficulties. In an unfamiliar place, it was also hard for her to find an accessible lift.

While working on our project, my classmates and I saw a father travelling with his autistic son. The MRT was very noisy, and the son covered his ears with both hands. I took a photo of the moment, thinking it might help with the project. When they reached their stop, the father asked me to delete the photo.

During our fieldwork, we noticed that other passengers often occupied accessible areas, making it difficult for wheelchair users to use them. The wheelchair area was not clearly marked, so it was easy for others to stand there without noticing.

We also noticed a large gap between the platform and the train, which could make getting on and off harder. Inside the carriage we observed, there was only one designated wheelchair space.

sections.name: 05 / FIRST DESIGN IDEA — Inspired by Escalator Lighting

children.text:
Our first idea came from the lights on escalators: green means you can go, and red means stop. We wondered if we could use light in a similar way on the MRT. When a wheelchair user needs to get off the train, floor lights in the wheelchair area would turn on to remind other passengers to give way.

We also thought about adding one more wheelchair space inside the carriage and marking the area in blue, a little like the priority seats. We hoped a clearer space would help passengers recognise who it is for and reduce people occupying it unnecessarily. This was our first concept, before we started testing and improving the design.

That encounter reminded me that fieldwork involves real people, not just examples for a design project. I should ask for permission before taking someone’s photo and respect their right not to be observed. Our research should not become another source of pressure.
Look beyond behaviour. Listen before making assumptions.

pages.title: LOOKING FOR THE REAL BARRIERS.
pages.intro: Starting our research with wheelchair users and public transport.

children.text: Our group began looking more closely at the travel experience of wheelchair users. We wanted to understand the journey as a whole, rather than focus on just one accessible facility.

We made a list of things to pay attention to: finding lifts, navigating signs, turning in narrow spaces, reaching service counters and using ticket or information machines. We also needed to think about the extra time and effort involved.
A station may have a lift or an accessible route, but can someone find and use it independently? This became one of the questions we wanted to explore in our fieldwork.

sections.name: 04 / MANY IDEAS · ONE SMALL MODEL / Photo Left Text Right

children.name: 04 / TURNING MESSY IDEAS INTO A MODEL

children.text: 04 / FROM IDEAS TO A SMALL MODEL

This was probably the week when we had the most ideas, and everything felt a bit messy. We had many things we wanted to try, but it was hard to explain them clearly. So we tried turning our ideas into a small model. We planned to show it to users and hear what they thought. Having something they could actually see would make it easier for us to explain the idea and get useful feedback.

sections.name: 05 / FIELD EXPERIMENT — From Flashing Lights to Softer Lighting

children.text: 05 / FIELD EXPERIMENT — TESTING OUR LIGHT IDEA

We tied LED strips around ourselves and went to the MRT to see how people would react. We wanted to find out whether passengers would notice the lights and give way when we were getting off the train.

During this little social experiment, we met a wheelchair user. We wanted to turn on the lights to help her board, but she asked where the lights would shine because bright light was uncomfortable for her eyes. That question made us realise that our idea of putting flashing lights near the train doors might not work for everyone.

I started thinking about people who look down at their phones or listen to music. How could we let them notice a change around them without using harsh flashing lights? Then I thought of aeroplanes. When I fall asleep on a flight, a gentle change in the cabin lighting often wakes me up without feeling too strong. So I suggested trying a softer, gradual change in lighting instead. We still needed to test whether it would work in the MRT.

pages.title: FROM PROBLEMS TO FIRST IDEAS.
pages.intro: Using our research to explore a clearer MRT wheelchair space.

children.text: We looked back at our MRT research and the wheelchair priority area. A space may be reserved for wheelchair users, but other passengers may not notice that it needs to be kept clear.

sections.name: Week 05 / Seven Photos Left · Our Early Idea Right

children.name: Week 05 / Tap for Next Photo (7 Independent Images)

children.text: Our group began exploring a way to mark the wheelchair area more clearly using gentle blue lighting. We wanted other passengers to notice the space without shining a spotlight on the wheelchair user or separating them from everyone else.

sections.name: 03 / INTERVIEW FINDINGS — Nikki, Mr Liang and Aqil

children.text: This week, we spoke with three wheelchair users: Nikki, Mr Liang and Aqil. Each interview made us look at our design from a different angle.

Nikki told us that she wanted to travel in the same carriage as other passengers. She didn’t want a separate carriage just for wheelchair users, like the women-only carriages in Japan. For her, being included in the same space was important.

children.name: MR LIANG / SIGNS PEOPLE CAN ACTUALLY NOTICE

children.text: MR LIANG / SIGNS PEOPLE CAN ACTUALLY NOTICE
Mr Liang didn’t know that the MRT had designated wheelchair spaces. This supported something we had noticed earlier: the accessible signs and markings were not clear enough for everyone to recognise.

Aqil suggested that we look at the lights used in newer Singapore ambulances. We went to see them and learned that the blue lighting was meant to create a calmer feeling. But to me, the blue was too strong and made my eyes uncomfortable. It made me think that lighting can affect people differently, so we need to test what actually feels comfortable.

sections.name: 03 / WHAT WE STILL NEEDED TO LEARN

children.text: 04 / WHAT WE STILL NEEDED TO LEARN
This was still an early idea, not a finished answer. We needed to understand whether the lighting would be clear, comfortable and useful for the people who actually use the area.
Find the problem first. Then test whether the idea really helps.

pages.title: RESEARCHING ACCESSIBILITY FOR DIFFERENT NEEDS.
pages.intro: After class, I looked at examples of how different spaces support Deaf people, wheelchair users, people with visual impairment and autistic people.

children.text: After class, I started looking for interior designs similar to the Deaf classroom we visited. I came across Gallaudet University’s DeafSpace ideas and found them really interesting. Some classrooms use a U-shaped or circular seating arrangement so people can see each other’s hands and facial expressions. The designs also consider wider walkways, clear views across a room and softer lighting without strong glare. Even mirrors and glass can help people notice someone approaching.

I looked at how MRT stations in Singapore use step-free routes, priority-use lift signs and wheelchair symbols. I also found a discussion by the Ministry of Transport about adding floor arrows to guide wheelchair users to lifts. The problem was that floor signs might be difficult to see when the platform is crowded.
CASE STUDY · TACTILE PATHS & AUDIO SIGNALS

I learned more about the tactile guiding system in MRT stations. The raised strips and dots can be felt with a white cane or under someone’s feet, helping them find important areas such as lifts, platforms and service counters. At some road crossings, audio signals also help people know when it is safe to cross.

children.name: Sources / VISUAL IMPAIRMENT / USING TOUCH & SOUND

children.text: I also found the Changi Airport Sensory Map, made to help visitors plan their journey and find quieter rest areas. Another example is the Calm Room at Terminal 2. It offers a place away from the busy airport, where people can take a break from overwhelming sights and sounds.

pages.title: SEEING MY HOMETOWN DIFFERENTLY.
pages.intro: A few observations from Guizhou, China, during the mid-semester break.

sections.name: 01 / GUIZHOU FIELD NOTES · Writing Left, Three Photos Right

children.text: 01 / A MOUNTAIN CITY I KNOW WELL

During the Week 08 break, I went back to my hometown in Guizhou, China. It is a small city that not many people know about, but if you love spicy food, you would probably fall in love with it.

My hometown is built among the mountains. There are a lot of underpasses, stairs and steps, and uneven roads are one of the biggest problems. After studying accessibility this semester, I began to notice how inconvenient some of these places could be for wheelchair users.

I saw a ramp blocked by a fence, which meant someone using a wheelchair could not actually use it to get down. On some pavements, stone bollards were placed to stop motorcycles from parking. But they could also get in the way of people trying to move along the pavement.

children.name: 02 / THE GOOD SIDE OF MY HOMETOWN

children.text: 02 / THE LITTLE THINGS THAT MAKE LIFE EASIER

Although I noticed some problems with accessibility, I also saw many good changes in my hometown. Tourism has been growing in Guizhou, and more services are making everyday life easier. For example, travellers can leave their luggage at some subway stations. I also saw rest stops made for delivery riders and street cleaners, with free drinking water inside.

And of course, I have to recommend my hometown’s food! If you like spicy food, Guizhou is definitely worth visiting. Moutai also comes from Guizhou, and coffee and beer have become popular in China too.

October is my favourite time to go back. The weather is cool, but the sunshine feels so warm on your skin.

This week, we started working on wayfinding for our exhibition. Our task was to guide visitors from Dhoby Ghaut MRT Station to the exhibition at Temasek Shophouse.

Before designing the route, we looked at many map references to see how different maps present directions, landmarks and useful information.

We also went to the area and took lots of photos along the way. We looked at station exits, crossings, lifts and walking paths.

pages.title: DRAWING OUR WAYFINDING MAPS.
pages.intro: A week of drawing, adjusting and trying to make our maps look like one set.

children.text: This week, we spent most of our time drawing the wayfinding maps. We were working together with the group focusing on autism. Since our group was not very familiar with Figma yet, we mainly took on the drawing work.

I didn’t expect drawing a map to take so much patience and attention to detail. We had to keep everything consistent, from the colours of the roads and different areas to the size of every little icon. Even small differences needed to be adjusted, so we spent a lot of time checking and changing things.

For our PD group, ramps and slopes were one of the main things we wanted to show on the map. The ASD group focused on different details, such as how noisy each area was and where visitors could stop and take a break.

Since we were working on the same wayfinding project, we needed to include both sets of information in our maps.

sections.name: 05 / USER INTERVIEWS — NOTES LEFT, THREE CLICKABLE PHOTOS RIGHT

children.text:
We took the different map designs above and showed them to wheelchair users and autistic users to hear their opinions. Some people liked maps that used different colours to separate information, while others preferred a clean and simple design.

But when we asked about the arrows, their choices were surprisingly similar. They all preferred a white arrow on a coloured circular background. I really didn’t expect that!

Now the difficult question is back on us: how can we bring all these different preferences together into one map?

sections.name: 06 / REAL PHOTOS & VIDEO GUIDANCE — TEXT LEFT / ONE PHOTO RIGHT

children.name: 06 / WHY WE STARTED FILMING THE ROUTE

children.text:
One problem with many navigation apps is that even when the map says you have arrived, you still might not know where the actual shop or entrance is. So we decided to add real photos and videos to our app, making it easier to recognise places along the route.

After our Week 10 interviews, three participants also said it would be much better if the videos had a real person showing where to go.

While working on the maps, we also started filming the route for our app.

We talked about Journey Mapping in class, and I started to think that the journey shouldn’t stop at a dot saying ‘arrived’. People still need to know which entrance to look for.

pages.title: PUTTING OUR MAPS TOGETHER.
pages.intro: From separate map drawings to one map, with new details for PD and ASD visitors.

children.text: This week, we finished our first map designs and started putting all the separate pieces together. Before that, everyone had been drawing different parts, so we needed to make them look and work like one map.

What makes our map a bit different is that we added information for both PD and ASD users. We used gradient colours to show ramps and slopes, and marked places where ASD visitors could stop and have a rest.

After our lecturer’s feedback, we added the video guidance and adjusted the arrow signs. We also decided to re-shoot the videos. Instead of a standing guide showing the way, we changed the view to that of a wheelchair user and a caregiver, so the directions would feel more relevant to them.

pages.title: WHAT IF THE BUTTON MOVED?
pages.intro: From ramps and lifts to a small question about how wheelchair users hold their phones.

children.text: From the observations and interviews over the past few weeks, I noticed two big problems for wheelchair users travelling somewhere unfamiliar: finding accessible ramps and finding the lifts. Even with a route on a map, it isn’t always easy to know exactly where these facilities are.

But I also noticed something when thinking about wheelchair users travelling alone. They may need one hand to hold their phone and the other to move the wheelchair. Looking down at a map and pressing small buttons at the same time could be really inconvenient. I started wondering if there was a better way to arrange the buttons.

My idea was quite simple: if someone holds their phone in their left hand, the main Next button could sit on the left. If they use their right hand, it could move to the right. And if they use a phone mount on their wheelchair, the Next button could be much bigger and easier to tap. I started looking at other navigation apps for ideas, but this layout was something I still wanted to explore, not a tested solution.

sections.name: 04 / APP RESEARCH — Wheelmap, AccessNow and Google Maps

children.text: I looked at how other apps show accessible places and routes. These are existing app screenshots, not my own designs. They gave me references for the map, while I wanted to focus more on how the buttons could work for someone travelling alone.

pages.title: ONE MORE APP BEFORE THE END.
pages.intro: Our group project was nearly ready, but I was still trying out my own wayfinding app.

children.text: By Week 13, most of our group project was already prepared, so there wasn’t much new fieldwork to do. We were mainly getting everything ready for the end of the semester.

sections.name: 02 / MY OWN WAYFINDING APP FOR WHEELCHAIR USERS

children.text:
With our group project almost ready, I also worked on my own navigation app called Wello, designed for wheelchair users. I wanted to think about more than just the map: how would someone actually use the app on their phone?

My main idea is the Adaptive Button Layout. Users can choose whether they hold their phone or have it on a phone mount attached to their wheelchair. They can also choose left-hand, right-hand or standard controls, so the buttons can suit how they use their phone.

The app adapts to the user, not the other way around.

children.text: 03 / WHAT I STILL WANT TO TEST
The next step is to ask wheelchair users to try different button positions. I want to see which layout feels easiest to tap and whether they need to change their posture to reach the buttons.
